overview: Side-by-side technical reference for Java, C++, and Python in Technical Interviews & Competitive Programming.

sections.concept: Contiguous resizable memory array with O(1) random access by index.

java.search: list.get(index); // O(1) by index, O(N) by value
java.pros: Type-safe, seamlessly integrates with Collections.sort() and Java Streams.
java.cons: Primitives incur boxing overhead (ArrayList<Integer> stores 24-byte Integer object references instead of 4-byte raw ints). For high-throughput CP, primitive int[] or FastIntArray is preferred.
java.pitfalls: Calling list.remove(1) removes index 1, NOT the integer value 1! To remove value 1, you must call list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)).

cpp.search: vec[index]; // O(1) without bounds check; vec.at(index) with bounds check
cpp.pros: Direct contiguous raw memory with zero boxing overhead. Highest cache locality and SIMD vectorization potential.
cpp.cons: Reallocation invalidates existing pointers and iterators.
cpp.pitfalls: Calling `vec.size() - 1` when vec is empty causes integer underflow because `size()` returns `size_t` (unsigned 64-bit integer), wrapping to 18446744073709551615!

python.pros: Extremely expressive syntax (slicing arr[::-1], list comprehensions [x*2 for x in arr]).
python.cons: High memory overhead (~8 bytes per pointer + PyObject overhead). Slower loop execution speed on competitive programming platforms.
python.pitfalls: Creating a 2D matrix via `[[0]*M]*N` creates N references to the EXACT SAME list in memory! Modifying `mat[0][0] = 1` mutates all rows! Always use `[[0]*M for _ in range(N)]`.

sections.concept: Key-value mapping providing O(1) average lookup, insertion, and deletion.

java.search: map.get(key); // O(1) average, returns null if missing
java.pros: Since Java 8, hash buckets that exceed 8 entries convert from linked lists to Red-Black balanced trees (O(log K) worst case), providing strong defense against collision attacks.
java.cons: Heavy memory footprint: each Map.Entry node object has ~32 bytes overhead.
java.pitfalls: Keys must properly override BOTH `equals()` and `hashCode()`. Overriding only one breaks hash bucket lookup silently.

cpp.insert: mp[key] = val; // or mp.insert({key, val}); O(1) average
cpp.pros: Fastest raw execution speed under normal random hashing conditions.
cpp.cons: Worst-case insertion is O(N) because std::unordered_map uses standard linked list chaining.
cpp.pitfalls: CRITICAL CODEFORCES TRAP: Codeforces users routinely craft test cases targeting `std::hash<long long>` (which is identity function `x % prime`). This causes all N elements to collide in bucket 0, degrading runtime to O(N^2) and causing Time Limit Exceeded (TLE). Always use a custom randomized hash like splitmix64!

python.pros: Since Python 3.7, dictionaries are guaranteed to maintain insertion order while retaining O(1) lookup.
python.cons: Slightly higher memory than C++ unordered_map.
python.pitfalls: Keys must be immutable (hashable). Attempting to use a mutable list as a dictionary key raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`. Use tuples `tuple(list)` instead.

sections.concept: Complete binary tree maintaining min or max element at root in O(1) access, O(log N) push/pop.

java.declaration:
PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(); // Min-heap by default
// Max-heap: new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());
java.pop: pq.poll(); // O(log N), returns null if empty
java.pros: Supports custom comparators easily: `new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] - b[0])`.
java.cons: Does not support decrease-key in O(log N) (remove(obj) is O(N)).
java.pitfalls: Using `(a, b) -> a - b` can cause integer overflow when subtracting large positive and negative numbers. Always use `Integer.compare(a, b)`.

cpp.declaration:
priority_queue<int> pq; // MAX-heap by default!
// Min-heap: priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> min_pq;
cpp.pros: Very fast cache-friendly contiguous array-backed binary heap.
cpp.cons: Default is MAX-heap (opposite of Java and Python!).
cpp.pitfalls: `pq.pop()` does NOT return the top element—it returns void! You must call `int top = pq.top();` first and then `pq.pop();`.

python.declaration:
import heapq
h = [] # Min-heap by default
python.pros: Transforms any standard Python list into a heap in-place in O(N) time using `heapq.heapify(h)`.
python.pitfalls: To implement a max-heap in Python, you must invert values (`-val`) on push and pop, or store tuples `(-priority, item)`. If storing tuples where priorities are equal, items must be comparable; otherwise pass unique index `(priority, index, item)`.

sections.concept: Optimizing input and output streams to handle up to 10^6 lines of text without TLE.

java.pitfall: Scanner uses regex matching internally and is 10x to 20x slower than BufferedReader. Avoid System.out.println() in large loops; use PrintWriter or StringBuilder.

cpp.pitfall: `std::endl` flushes the stream on every single line, turning O(N) output into O(N) blocking system calls. Always use `'\n'` instead of `std::endl`.

python.snippet:
import sys

# Fast I/O
input = sys.stdin.readline

# Increase recursion depth for deep graph DFS / tree traversals
sys.setrecursionlimit(300000)

def main():
    line = input().strip()
    # sys.stdout.write(str(ans) + '\n') for fastest output
python.pitfall: Default recursion limit in Python is only 1,000 frames. Deep DFS on trees with N = 10^5 will crash with RecursionError. Always call `sys.setrecursionlimit(300000)` or rewrite recursion iteratively.
